title: Draft well interference policy and Mannheim water update
subtitle: Appeal committee makeup, Mannheim treatment progress, water allocation to municipalities, and next steps toward a September policy report
overview: At this special meeting on water, Council received two reports for information. Staff updated Council on the Mannheim service area water capacity constraint, including the arrival of a modular treatment unit for the Mannheim side stream project. Water allocation agreements are signed with four area municipalities, and Wilmot is to consider its agreement in August.

Council also reviewed a draft policy for groundwater interference complaints. It would replace a single decision maker with a five-member appeal committee, remove fixed compensation limits and the historic compensation zone, and use an independent consultant and licensed well technician to assess complaints. A delegate from Wilmot asked that independent members of the public sit on the committee.

No policy decision was made. Councillors asked staff to return with more options on committee membership, wording that covers businesses and farms, and legal advice on remedies and burden of proof. A public information session is planned for August 20, and a final policy and draft terms of reference are due back on September 9, 2026. The only motion that changed anything was the enactment of by-laws {{vote:m1}}, and the meeting then adjourned {{vote:m2}}.

decisions.detail: Council gave first, second and third readings to the by-laws, confirming the day's proceedings, with both water reports received for information only {{vote:m1}}.

debate: A Wilmot delegate said the appeal committee should include independent members of the public, rather than only people tied to the Region, and cited ongoing worry about well water.

Several councillors supported adding a community member, possibly non-voting and appointed on a multi-year term, noting that few elected officials own private wells. Others questioned having five councillors on the committee and suggested an independent professional or an elected official from another municipality.

Staff said they left out public members for independence, privacy and because Council approves remedies. They noted that the Guelph committee has no public members and that the consultant and well technician are bound by professional obligations. One councillor said a mostly political committee could help for its first term, and another doubted that extra technical members would add value.

Councillors raised concerns about requiring residents to sign a final acknowledgement and pay for remedy work up front, and asked that the burden of proof stay with the Region through appeals. Staff said legal advice on these points would come back in September.

One councillor asked whether removing the compensation cap makes costs unpredictable. Staff said an initial screening limits which cases go forward and gave a range of possible remedy costs, from minor pump changes to new wells.
